stated.value: We already have a fluorescence spectrometer and would like to use it
We have not identified a fluorescent target, marker or reference relationship
report glucose concentration and viable biomass directly during fermentation

missing: Organism and medium composition of the fermentation
Expected glucose concentration range and required accuracy
Definition of 'viable biomass' and the laboratory method used to measure it
Process conditions at the probe point (temperature, pressure, sterilisation/cleaning, port size)
Specification of the existing fluorescence spectrometer (excitation source, wavelength range)

status_reason: Material (fermentation), quantities (glucose, viable biomass) and location (in the fermenter) are known, but fluorescence alone cannot be approved for glucose because the sources assign glucose to Raman and NIR, and viable biomass still needs a defined signal and an independent viability reference.
answer: Fluorescence is sensitive but not selective, and in the supplied bioprocess material it measures intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, not glucose, so your spectrometer should not be used to report glucose. Glucose should be tested with Raman (direct metabolite detection in aqueous media) against NIR, while your fluorescence spectrometer may contribute to a biomass estimate in combination with NIR, which improved biomass determination in yeast fermentation. Viable biomass first needs an independent viability reference before any spectroscopic model can be built.

inline.headline: Test Raman for glucose in fermentation samples first, compared with NIR, before any in-line installation.
inline.probe: Raman fiber probe in contact with the broth
inline.install: unknown – ask (port in the fermenter or a bypass loop, to be defined with the client)
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica (350–2400 nm), Al/Cu-coated to avoid polymer-jacket fluorescence
inline.not_final_because: Organism, medium, glucose range, required accuracy, probe-point conditions and the viable-biomass reference are unknown, Raman can be masked by strong fluorescence of organic compounds, and a published application is only a reason to test.

problems.text: High sensitivity is not selectivity: fluorescence is rated high in sensitivity but low in selectivity, works only for substances that fluoresce (most chemicals do not), and combined-probe work is limited to samples with at least one fluorescent component.
There is no direct fluorescence route to glucose in the sources: fluorescence targets NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and reference: the sources link biomass to turbidity (cell density) and report NIR plus fluorescence improving biomass in yeast fermentation, but describe no viable-cell measurement, so an independent viability reference is required.
Any fluorescence or Raman result will need a chemometric model built and validated against independent laboratory references, because fluorescence spectra are broad and overlapping.

methods.why: Gives direct detection of glucose, acetate or lactate and suits aqueous media because water absorbs weakly.
Tracks major components such as glucose in the millimolar range and, combined with fluorescence, improved biomass estimates in yeast fermentation.
Your existing spectrometer can follow intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin as a contribution to a biomass/metabolic-state model, not as a glucose sensor.
Can be a low-cost biomass indicator because turbidity correlates with cell density, which is total cells rather than viable cells.

questions.q: Which organism and medium do you ferment, and what glucose range do you need to measure?
questions.why: NIR may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %, so the range decides between NIR and Raman.

questions.q: How do you define viable biomass and which laboratory method measures it today?
questions.why: The sources describe no viable-cell measurement, so an independent reference is needed to build any model.

questions.q: What excitation source and wavelength range does your fluorescence spectrometer have?
questions.why: Fluorescence targets such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin must be excitable and the fiber must transmit the range.

questions.q: Where could a probe be installed and what temperature, pressure and cleaning/sterilisation does it face?
questions.why: Probe and fiber choice depend on the interface and conditions; coated silica fibers offer high-temperature resistance.

questions.q: What accuracy and response time would make the measurement useful for you?
questions.why: These go/no-go criteria are needed to judge whether a validated model is good enough.

technical.spectral_window: Raman: excitation 785 nm (as used in AFS examples), Raman shift range unknown – ask/determine in lab test; NIR 780–2500 nm; fluorescence under UV/visible excitation, range unknown – ask
technical.probe: Raman fiber probe and NIR transmission/transflection probe (1–10 mm path); tip/window material unknown – ask
technical.fiber: Vis-NIR silica 350–2400 nm (UV-Vis silica 190–1200 nm for fluorescence), Al/Cu-coated for Raman/fluorescence; length and routing unknown – ask
technical.reference_method: Independent laboratory glucose analysis and a viable-cell reference method; both unknown – ask
technical.calibration: Fermentation samples spanning the client's glucose and biomass ranges with independent reference values; ranges unknown – ask

experiment.objective: Determine whether Raman or NIR sees glucose changes in the client's fermentation samples and whether fluorescence adds information for biomass.
steps: Collect fermentation samples across the run covering the expected glucose and biomass ranges, each with independent laboratory glucose and viable-cell references.
Record Raman, NIR and fluorescence spectra of the same samples with fiber probes in the AFS multi-method lab test.
Identify key spectral features that change with glucose and with biomass by multivariate analysis.
Build and validate single-method chemometric models and a fused NIR + fluorescence biomass model on the same validation data.
references: Independent laboratory glucose analysis (method to be named by the client)
Independent viable-cell measurement (method to be named by the client)
experiment.go_no_go: Accuracy and response-time criteria come from the client (unknown – ask).

pathway.key_features: No spectra supplied; key features for glucose and biomass are to be identified in the lab test.
pathway.path_reason: The method and the viable-biomass reference are not yet established, so no tailored solution can be chosen before the multi-method lab test.

multispectral.why: NIR tracks major components while fluorescence follows intrinsic fluorophores of the cells' metabolic state, and the combination gave more accurate biomass in yeast fermentation.
multispectral.probe: separate synchronised probes (a combined same-spot probe is needed only if the broth proves heterogeneous)
multispectral.fusion: model per method first, then data fusion with dedicated algorithms
multispectral.test: The fused model must predict the independent biomass reference better than the best single method on the same validation data.

assumptions: The fermentation broth is an aqueous liquid medium.
The client can provide samples with independent laboratory references for glucose and viable cells.
